segments.text: This demo compares SHA-3-256, the compact core in this project, and Oxide's Quartz implementation.
Here's how the input architecture changes speed and resource use.
Start with Oxide's Quartz SHA-3-256 core. One byte arrives each clock. Two block
buffers let it fill the next block while processing the previous one. That's a good
match for its byte stream workload. With the full rate adapter, this integration
reaches nearly a hundred megabytes per second. The compact core takes the wider path. DMA already
delivers eight bytes at a time. A small buffer feeds those bytes straight into the hash state.
Both full block buffers disappear. The digest reads the state itself. Capture and absorption
still take separate cycles, and the permutation still takes 24 rounds. The next step was
simplifying the surrounding logic. Padding only touches 17 lanes, so the selector doesn't need
to reach across all 25. Framing errors are also registered before updating the state.
The compact version keeps the same simulated cycle count, with fewer standalone lookup tables.
Here are the routed SHA-3-256 resource counts. About 23% fewer lookup tables,
58% fewer flip-flops. Those totals include the local adapters, so the comparison covers the
complete routed hash partitions. Both use zero block RAM and zero DSP blocks. Both cores use
the same board, shell, driver, and 100 megahertz clock. The comparison uses the median of seven
samples after warm-up, with every digest checked against software. Upload and reconfiguration
are outside these timers. Now compare SHA-3-256 hashing time for a 16.8 megabyte message.
Oxide's quartz takes about 169 milliseconds. The compact core takes 72. That's 2.36 times
the DMA throughput. Through the processing system API, the gain is 1.91 times, with copying and
request overheads still included. Oxide's quartz still wins the small requests in these measurements.
This improvement applies to large buffers on this board. The reserved region and image size are
unchanged. Power and oxide production system performance weren't measured. Thanks to Oxide
and the quartz contributors for making the reference available, their unchanged source
and license are retained alongside the measurements. The project was developed with AI assistance.
Now, onto the board. Now, a SHA-3-256 check on the physical board. First,
the dashboard checks the connected ZYBO. Next, select the 8.2 kilobyte sample and send it to
the FPGA. The processing system feeds DMA and the compact core does the hashing. The
dashboard compares the result with an independent PC reference. And there it is. The two digests
match. That's onboard hash time. The USB upload is excluded. This is a fresh correctness check,
separate from the benchmark. The original hash profile is ready for another file.
